narrative:
The model estimates a 40% chance that you will leave your job. Because of this moderate risk, the company has decided not to approve your promotion at this time.

Three factors shaped this prediction most strongly. First, the model placed the greatest weight on the fact that you have spent more than 11 years in your current organization. Among employees the model expects to stay, only 14% have been with their employer this long. Long tenure in one place often signals that someone may be ready for a change, and that pattern pulled the prediction toward leaving.

The second most important factor was that you have received other job offers while working here. This is relatively uncommon—only 23% of employees the model sees as likely to stay have outside opportunities—yet it clearly increases the chance you might depart.

Finally, your high level of emotional commitment to the organization worked in the opposite direction. Strong loyalty is more common among people expected to remain, and this factor helped push the prediction back toward staying, though not enough to outweigh the first two influences.

The company should discuss your long service, the external offers you have received, and ways to strengthen your sense of future growth here. You may want to reflect on whether your current role still matches your career goals. Addressing these points openly could either reduce the risk of departure or lead to a better-matched opportunity. (238 words)
